title: Why does heartbreak hurt so much?
reason: 昨天的课程聚焦消费决策，今天轮换到日常生活与人际沟通。本集以脑科学解释亲密关系、社会联结和失恋带来的真实感受，既贴近日常经验，也适合练习用清楚、常用的表达说明因果关系与健康影响。练习通过重复调用高频词组，逐步把被动理解转化为主动输出。

targetExpressions.meaning: remember and consider a time or event in the past
targetExpressions.usage: Use it to introduce a past example: Think back to a time when a friend supported you.

targetExpressions.meaning: begin to feel romantic love for someone
targetExpressions.usage: Use it for the start of a romantic relationship: The programme examines what happens in the brain when people fall in love.

targetExpressions.meaning: depend strongly on someone or something and want more of them or it
targetExpressions.usage: It can be literal or metaphorical: The expert says humans are biologically driven to be addicted to each other.

targetExpressions.meaning: have someone or something as your main focus
targetExpressions.usage: Use it to describe attention or priorities: A person in love may be oriented towards their partner.

targetExpressions.meaning: close relationships with family, friends or romantic partners
targetExpressions.usage: Use it to discuss supportive relationships: Strong social bonds can help people manage stress.

targetExpressions.meaning: make an outcome more probable for you
targetExpressions.usage: Use it to explain a positive or negative effect: Regular practice can increase your likelihood of remembering new expressions.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete Neil's opening request: “I want you to ______ the last time you had your heart broken.”
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Neil uses “think back to” to ask Georgie to remember a past experience.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: What did scientists find when they scanned the brains of people looking at a romantic partner?

options.text: A brain area linked to basic needs such as eating and drinking became active.
Every part of the brain stopped responding to physical needs.
Only the areas used for solving mathematical problems became active.
The brain treated the partner as a completely unknown person.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The transcript says that looking at someone you are in love with activates a brain area that also reminds us to eat and drink.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete Dr Lucy Brown's explanation: Nature gave humans systems to ______ each other for reproduction and protection.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Dr Brown describes romantic love as a survival system that makes humans “be addicted to each other”.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: In the programme, what does it mean to “be oriented towards” another person?

options.text: Make that person a main focus and think of them before others.
Avoid thinking about that person in any situation.
Compete with that person for food and water.
Study the geographical direction in which the person is travelling.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The vocabulary recap defines oriented or orientated towards as having someone or something as your main focus.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Which example best matches the programme's meaning of “social bonds”?

options.text: Close, supportive relationships with family, friends or partners.
Short-term financial products sold by a bank.
A list of strangers seen once on public transport.
Rules that prevent people from speaking to each other.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: The programme defines social bonds as close relationships with family, friends and romantic partners.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Complete Professor Donaldson's point: Strong social bonds ______ surviving many different difficulties.
objectiveQuestions.explanation: Professor Donaldson says strong social bonds increase the likelihood that a person will survive many kinds of difficulty. The version with “your” directly practises today's target expression.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: What is the theory connecting children's early bonds with parents to their adult romantic relationships?
objectiveQuestions.explanation: The quiz answer is attachment theory, developed from observations about early parent-child bonds and later relationships.

objectiveQuestions.prompt: Which sentence uses “think back to” naturally?

options.text: Think back to a time when a close friend helped you through a difficult week.
I think back the report to my manager tomorrow.
She thinks the meeting back to finish early.
We are think back to the new server every day.

objectiveQuestions.explanation: “Think back to” is followed by a past time, event or experience that someone is asked to remember.

subjectiveQuestions.gradingCriteria: A supported answer should say that the romantic partner becomes the person's main focus or is considered before other people. assessment.retellingPrompt: Without looking at the full transcript, retell the episode in 80–120 words using this structure: (1) what happens in the brain when people fall in love; (2) two benefits of strong relationships; (3) why heartbreak can feel like physical pain. Phrase bank: “fall in love”, “social bonds”, “increase your likelihood of”. Use at least two phrases naturally. Simple, accurate sentences are enough.
referencePoints: Brain scans show that seeing a romantic partner activates a brain area also connected with basic needs such as eating and drinking.
Dr Lucy Brown describes romantic love as a survival system linked to reproduction and protection.
People in love may make their partner a main focus, and brain activity can treat statements about the partner similarly to statements about the self.
Good social connections may help manage stress and support the immune system.
Strong social bonds are associated with a greater chance of survival and are a major predictor of longevity.
Looking at an ex can activate brain regions associated with danger and physical pain, helping explain why heartbreak can hurt physically.
